Name: linguistic_cost_of_thought

novelty.reasoning: Core novel claims: (1) redefining language-agnosticism as a per-step, time-varying 'linguistic cost meter' during reasoning; (2) linking higher step difficulty to stronger language-shedding; (3) using that signal to gate steering only on hard steps; (4) claiming gated steering beats blanket language ablation on the accuracy/fluency tradeoff; (5) using LAS as a correctness predictor. The closest prior family is static/global language ablation and English-routing/core-representation work, plus recent shared-difficulty-geometry and probe-based correctness prediction. The actual delta is real but narrower than it first sounds: the H1-style difficulty/representation link is partly anticipated, and H2 is below the bar of existing probes. The strongest potential novelty lives in the intervention/gating mechanism and its comparative tradeoff result, if it holds.
revision_notes: State the exact novelty claim in one sentence: per-step difficulty-gated steering improves multilingual reasoning more than static ablation under matched compute and intervention budget.
Explicitly distinguish the work from shared-difficulty-geometry by clarifying that you test temporal dynamics and causal gating, not just a shared difficulty direction.
Remove or de-emphasize the correctness-prediction claim unless you can show a new use case beyond existing high-AUROC probes.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is whether reasoning difficulty correlates with transient language-shedding in multilingual LLMs, and whether exploiting that signal improves multilingual reasoning. Researchers in multilingual reasoning, interpretability, and inference-time control would care; practitioners care if it improves accuracy without harming fluency or target-language output. The strongest one-line case is: if reasoning difficulty can be detected online from hidden-state language-agnosticism, we can intervene only when needed instead of bluntly suppressing language features everywhere. Importance is moderate-to-high but not field-shifting unless gains are clear and robust. Yes, serious researchers would care if the result comes out either way, but mainly as a mechanistic/controls result rather than an application breakthrough.
revision_notes: Add a concrete downstream scenario showing why adaptive gating matters more than blanket ablation (e.g., preserving fluency/cost while improving multilingual math accuracy).
Quantify the expected tradeoff improvement that would make practitioners switch from static to gated intervention.
Broaden evaluation to at least one real user-facing setting beyond benchmark QA/math, if feasible.

review.reasoning: The proposal is testable and reasonably scoped, but the central claims are not yet tight enough. There is a logical gap between a projection onto a language-identity subspace and the interpretation 'cost of thought'; content confounds could drive the signal. The falsifiable hypothesis is present, but the operationalization of difficulty is weakly defined and may not isolate true reasoning difficulty from token entropy, language mixing, or prompt artifacts. Related work is adequate at a high level but needs sharper positioning against the 2026 probe and shared-difficulty papers. Experiments are mostly feasible and include some good controls (random-gated, blanket ablation), but missing are stronger causal controls, calibration of LAS against trivial baselines, and ablations showing the signal is not just length/entropy. Minimum viable edits: tighten definitions, pre-register primary endpoints, add stronger controls, and make the intervention budget strictly comparable across methods.

Name: syntax_engine_reuse

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) a previously localized hierarchy-selective language circuit is causally reused for non-linguistic hierarchical reasoning; (2) ablation should show a depth-by-ablation interaction on arithmetic/logic/parentheses/code; (3) independently localized reasoning circuits should overlap with the syntax circuit; (4) LoRA on nested reasoning should strengthen the syntax circuit. Relative to prior work, the delta is real and specific: prior circuit-localization work only tested language grammaticality, while adjacent shared-circuit studies were on other domains and no one had directly causally tested reuse of the syntax circuit on non-linguistic hierarchy. Novelty is strongest in the causal test and setting, not in the general reuse idea.
revision_notes: Sharpen the novelty claim around the exact circuit identity and operational definition so it is clear this is not just another mechanistic interpretability ablation paper.
Explicitly contrast against the dissociation literature and state what result would be surprising under domain-separation views.

State why the four task families are the minimal set needed to establish general reuse rather than task-specific transfer.

impact.reasoning: The underlying phenomenon is whether syntax-specific machinery in LLMs is a general-purpose structure engine. That matters to interpretability, cognitive science, and reasoning-mechanism work, and it directly informs the language-vs-thought debate. The strongest one-line case: if syntax circuits are reused for non-linguistic hierarchy, then a major class of reasoning may be explainable as repurposed linguistic machinery; if not, that strengthens modularity/dissociation. This is not a niche curiosity, but uptake depends on the result because either outcome would be informative for how people model structure processing in LLMs.

The experiments are feasible and mostly appropriate, but the proposal needs stronger falsifiability around what pattern would count as reuse versus generic degradation. Executed well, this could be a serious ML venue paper, especially because both positive and negative results are informative.

Name: linguistic_cognitive_gear

novelty.reasoning: Core claims that need to be novel are: (1) prompt surface language can shift an LLM's decision strategy on identical problems along an intuition-vs-reflection axis; (2) this appears across a multilingual battery of dual-process-style bias tasks rather than a single benchmark; (3) the effect dissociates from overall accuracy and language resource level; (4) there exists a locatable linear 'reflection direction' mediating the language effect; (5) causal steering along that direction can override language-induced intuitive answers. Relative to the search summary, the dual-process framing itself is not new, cognitive-bias measurement/mitigation in LLMs is already active, and steering/System-1/2 directions already exist. The most defensible novelty is the cross-language dissociation on matched items plus tying it to a causal representation-level intervention. The proposal is more than an obvious baseline comparison, but the chosen human FLE framing is shaky for this bias battery, and some of the mechanistic pieces look like a natural extension of existing probing/steering work rather than a wholly new mechanism.
revision_notes: Reframe the novelty claim away from importing the contested human Foreign Language Effect and toward a distinctly LLM-specific multilingual strategy-routing phenomenon.
State the exact closest prior families and the delta explicitly: multilingual reasoning accuracy papers, single-bias language effects, and System-1/2 probing/steering papers.

Add one setting or task component that is clearly not covered by prior bias batteries, e.g. tightly controlled same-semantic-content cross-language switches within model/item, or cross-script/code-switch conditions.
Clarify whether the main novelty is the finding, the mechanism, or the causal intervention, and narrow claims accordingly.
Strengthen the mechanism beyond a generic linear probe by specifying what would distinguish a true reflection-direction account from simple language/difficulty separability.

impact.reasoning: The problem under study is whether multilingual prompt language changes which reasoning strategy an LLM deploys, leading to language-dependent susceptibility to intuitive lures even when task semantics are unchanged. This matters to multilingual-NLP, interpretability, and reliability/safety researchers, and to practitioners deploying LLMs across languages. The strongest case is: if prompt language systematically shifts reasoning mode, multilingual evaluations and deployments cannot treat translation-equivalent prompts as behaviorally equivalent. The phenomenon is meaningful and could affect benchmarking, prompting, and mitigation. That said, the direct practical reach depends on effect size and generality; the selected bias tasks are somewhat narrow and the result may mostly interest research communities unless connected more clearly to deployed workflows. The 'so what?' test is partially passed: a robust effect either way would influence multilingual evaluation methodology and some prompting/steering work, but may not broadly change production practice unless shown on more consequential tasks.
revision_notes: Make the practical consequence concrete: specify how multilingual evaluation, prompt design, or safety auditing would change if the effect is confirmed or rejected.

review.reasoning: The proposal is testable and more concrete than many idea sketches, but several technical gaps remain. The main hypothesis is reasonably falsifiable, yet 'intuition-vs-reflection axis' is underoperationalized and heavily dependent on a contested mapping from lure responses to cognitive mode. The related work is directionally aware but not specific enough about the strongest nearest baselines from multilingual LLM bias and System-1/2 steering. Experimental design has promising controls (mixed effects, random steering controls, answer-language fidelity), but key confounds remain: translation naturalness, item difficulty shifts, cultural familiarity, tokenization/script effects, and CoT responsiveness as a proxy for reflection. Intuition Index=lure rate among errors may be unstable and can miss language effects that change both error type and accuracy. The probe experiment risks detecting answer class, language identity, or difficulty instead of reflection; causal steering mid-layer may improve performance through generic logit biasing rather than mechanism-specific intervention. The story also overclaims by borrowing human FLE motivation for tasks where human evidence is largely null. If executed well with stronger controls, it could be workshop-to-mid-tier conference material and possibly stronger if the mechanistic evidence is convincing, but in current form it is not yet submission-ready for a serious top ML venue.

Name: token_granularity_reasoning_tradeoff

novelty.reasoning: Core technical claims needing novelty are: (1) coarse vs fine tokenization induces a unified fluency/retrieval vs compositional-reasoning trade-off on the same strings; (2) this trade-off is mediated by a per-concept 'granularity depth' where sub-token structure becomes linearly decodable; (3) granularity depth shifts systematically with token coarseness/frequency and predicts downstream reasoning failures; (4) a training-free steering method, STRS, can amplify sub-token reconstruction at the breakthrough layer to move along this trade-off at inference. Relative to prior work, the breakthrough-layer reconstruction phenomenon is already known, and STRS is a natural extension of existing steering methods. The most defensible novelty is the unifying trade-off framing plus an inference-time control lever. The per-concept diagnostic is incremental unless it yields a genuinely new predictive law beyond re-measuring established reconstruction effects.
revision_notes: State the closest prior work family explicitly and rewrite each claimed contribution as a concrete delta over that work, especially inner-lexicon/breakthrough-layer papers and steering baselines.

Add at least one non-obvious comparison showing STRS is not just equivalent to forced fine tokenization or generic activation steering.
Define whether novelty lies in the finding, mechanism, diagnostic, or intervention, and avoid implying all four are equally new.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is the effect of token granularity on a model's ability to manipulate internal structure while preserving fluent retrieval. Relevant audiences include tokenization researchers, reasoning-mechanism researchers, multilingual/vocabulary-design practitioners, and model efficiency practitioners. If true, the work could influence how people choose vocabularies, evaluate reasoning under tokenization, and deploy inference-time mitigations. The strongest case is that it unifies two influential but seemingly conflicting tokenization literatures and offers a practical training-free knob. The 'so what?' test is moderately positive: if the result holds strongly, researchers may rethink vocabulary design and add tokenization-sensitive evaluations; if it fails, many would likely continue using existing tokenization heuristics, so direction-shifting potential is real but not guaranteed.

Add a sharper claim about how a null result would still matter, for example by falsifying the notion that inference-time access to sub-token structure can recover reasoning without retraining.

review.reasoning: The proposal is coherent and fairly well scoped, with falsifiable hypotheses and a sensible experimental arc. However, key technical gaps remain. 'Fluency' is weakly operationalized via perplexity plus judged quality, which may not capture the claimed retrieval/fluency construct. The causal story from decodability to reasoning ability is still correlational unless interventions are carefully localized and alternative explanations ruled out. The tokenization manipulations may confound granularity with sequence length, formatting, and token identity effects. Granularity depth uses an arbitrary 80% threshold and linear decodability may reflect probe artifacts rather than actual accessibility. STRS as difference-in-means reconstruction direction is underspecified and may entangle semantic/content shifts. Related work is reasonably specific but overclaims absence of prior reconciliation. If executed strongly, this could be a respectable ML mechanisms/tokenization paper, but it currently needs tighter definitions, controls, and stronger baselines to be submission-ready.

Name: verbal_interference_llm

novelty.reasoning: Core claims needing novelty are: (1) a new evaluation problem—identify which LLM reasoning tasks depend on language production machinery; (2) a new mechanism/method—Concurrent Linguistic Load (CLL), importing human dual-task verbal-interference logic rather than ablation or verbalization removal; (3) a predicted task-by-load selective impairment gradient across task families; (4) a circuit-level claim that CLL cost tracks overlap with language-production components; and (5) a distinction between genuine linguistic competition versus generic token/context overhead via graded and control loads. Relative to prior work, the main novelty is methodological: loading/competition instead of ablation, plus graded controls. The broader question (language vs thought in LLMs) is not new, and the search summary indicates very close prior work already localizes language-relevant units and finds broad dependence of verbally presented tasks on them, which weakens the headline dissociation claim. The proposal's own related work underspecifies this closest family, making the delta seem larger than it is. Still, if executed well, the selective dual-task paradigm and competition-based interpretation are non-trivial and not just an obvious baseline swap.
revision_notes: Explicitly position against ablation/localization papers on LLM language networks and state the precise methodological delta: competition-under-load versus lesion-based necessity.
Narrow the novelty claim from 'reveal dissociation between language and reasoning' to 'test for selective competition signatures beyond non-specific impairment'.
Define what is novel at each level: paradigm (CLL), finding (task-by-load interaction), mechanism (shared language-production bottleneck), and setting (multi-model frozen LLMs).
Add a table comparing CLL to closest baselines: ablation of language units, hidden-state reasoning suppression/removal, longer-context overhead controls, and generic dual-output prompting.

Pre-register an outcome where even a negative result is novel: failure to find selective interference despite strong controls would challenge the human analogy and refine language-vs-thought claims in LLMs.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is whether LLM performance on different reasoning tasks actually depends on language-production machinery, not merely whether a new prompt trick works. Who cares: LLM-cognition researchers, mechanistic interpretability, benchmark designers, and anyone making claims about latent reasoning or language-independent thought in models. If the result holds cleanly, it could affect how people evaluate reasoning, interpret verbal chain-of-thought, and design probes for modularity or resource competition. The strongest case is that it offers a more behaviorally grounded test of language dependence than lesions alone. The 'so what?' test is mixed but positive: if selective interference appears, researchers would likely revise claims about which tasks are truly language-mediated and use load-based controls in future work; if all tasks degrade non-specifically, that would still matter but less dramatically, mainly as a caution about anthropomorphic analogies and prompt-based concurrency. Real-world reach is moderate rather than high, because this is mostly foundational/diagnostic rather than directly product-changing.

Strengthen the one-line importance claim around adjudicating whether LLM 'reasoning' is separable from language production under controlled competition.

Include at least one application-facing implication, e.g., diagnosing when multiturn assistant behavior is vulnerable to concurrent generation demands or verbosity constraints.

review.reasoning: The proposal is testable and reasonably structured, but several core claims are currently under-defended. The biggest logical gap is whether prompt interleaving constitutes meaningful 'concurrent load' rather than simply added decoding burden, longer contexts, or instruction-format interference. Controls help, but may not isolate linguistic competition cleanly because all conditions still consume the same autoregressive channel. H1 is fairly falsifiable via task-by-load interaction, but the task taxonomy ('language-heavy' to 'abstract') is only hypothesized and needs operationalization independent of the results. H3 is the weakest part: 'language-production components' via next-token fluency attribution and overlap via activation patching are underspecified, and correlation between CLL cost and overlap could be confounded by generic task difficulty, sequence length, or shared decoder usage. Related work is not positioned specifically enough given very close prior work. Experimental design is feasible, but missing key controls: same-token-budget non-fluent loads, paraphrase/format variants, answer-position controls, and analyses separating accuracy loss from compliance failure. As written, this feels like a solid workshop/early-stage mechanistic study, but not yet strong enough for a top ML venue without tighter hypotheses and stronger controls.

review.reasoning: The proposal is testable and reasonably scoped, but several claims are overloaded and some controls are still underspecified. The main hypothesis is falsifiable, yet the proposed interpretation risks conflating grammar with length, salience, semantic framing, and model prior biases. Related work is adequate but should more explicitly engage the recent human evidence that reverses the expected sign. Experiments are plausible and partially controlled, especially with within-item framing and random-direction controls, but key details are missing: exact prompt templates, pre-registered primary estimand, power/precision targets, probe validation, and how steering directions will be separated from reward magnitude or generic sentiment. A serious venue paper is plausible if executed well, but the proposal needs tighter hypothesis separation and a more defensive analysis plan.
